en: The Tārasāropaniṣad: That which is the form of truth, knowledge, and bliss— the meaning of Nārāyaṇa and Tārā—
consisting of three feet and having Nārāyaṇa as its source, that Brahman alone am I.
Oṃ. That is fullness, this is fullness; from fullness, fullness arises.
When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Hariḥ Oṃ.

Bṛhaspati said to Yājñavalkya: "Kurukṣetra is the sacrificial ground of the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings; therefore, wherever one may go, one should consider that very place to be so. This indeed is Kurukṣetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods."
The place of sacrifice for the gods, the seat of Brahman for all beings— here, indeed,
when the vital breaths of a creature depart, Rudra reveals the saving Brahman,
by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation. Therefore, one should devote oneself solely to Avimukta.
"One should not release what has not been released. "It is even so, O Blessed One," said Yājñavalkya. || 1 ||

Then Bhāradvāja asked Yājñavalkya: "What is the Tāraka? What does it deliver? Yājñavalkya replied: "One should worship 'Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya' as the Tāraka, which is of the nature of consciousness (cidātmaka). 'Oṃ' is the single syllable, the very form of the Self."
The two syllables "namaḥ" are the nature of Prakṛti; the five syllables "nārāyaṇāya" are the nature of the Supreme Brahman. He who knows this becomes immortal. The syllable "oṃ" is Brahmā;
the letter "na" is Viṣṇu; the letter "ma" is Rudra; the letter "na" is Īśvara.
The letter *ra* becomes the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), the Virāj; the letter *ya* becomes the Puruṣa; the letter *ṇa* becomes the Blessed One (*bhagavān*);
the letter *ya* becomes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This indeed is the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa, which is the Supreme Person of the Vedas. This is the first foot of the Ṛgveda. || 1 ||

"Oṃ"—this syllable is the supreme Brahman; it alone is to be meditated upon. This very [syllable] becomes the subtle eight-syllabled [mantra]. That same [mantra], consisting of eight aspects, becomes eightfold. The letter *a* is the first syllable; the letter *u* is the second syllable.

The letter *ma* is the third syllable; the *bindu* is the fourth syllable; the *nāda* is the fifth syllable; the *kalā* is the sixth syllable; the *kalātītā* is the seventh syllable; and that which is beyond that (*tatpara*) is the eighth syllable.
Because it delivers [one] across, it is the "Deliverer" (tāraka). Know that this very Deliverer is Brahman;
that alone is to be meditated upon. On this point, there are these verses:
From the letter *a* arose Brahmā, known by the name Jāmbavān;
from the letter *u* was born Upendra, the leader of the Haris.
Śiva, born from the syllable *m*, is remembered as Hanumān;
the *bindu* is named Īśvara, and Śatrughna is himself the sovereign of the wheel (*cakrarāj*).
The great lord Nāda should be known as Bharata, named Śaṅkha;
he is the manifest Puruṣa of Kalā, Lakṣmaṇa, the upholder of the earth. || 3 ||
The Blessed Lady herself, who transcends all time, is known by the name Sītā;
and the Supreme Self, Śrī Rāma, the Puruṣottama, is devoted to her. || 4 ||

"Om"—this single syllable is all this. Its detailed explanation is as follows: it is the past, the present, and the future; and whatever else exists, consisting of reality, mantras, phonemes, deities, meters, verses, parts, powers, and creation. He who knows thus [attains this].
The Yajurveda is the second foot. || 2 ||
Then Bhāradvāja said to Yājñavalkya: "Now, by which mantras does the Supreme Self become pleased and reveal His own self? Tell us that, O Blessed One. Yājñavalkya replied:
Oṃ! He who is indeed the glorious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed Lord denoted by the syllable *A*, Jāmbavān—the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—to him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. || 1 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed the illustrious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed Lord denoted by the syllable *u*, whose nature is Upendra, the leader Hari—to Him, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, we offer salutations again and again. || 2 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed the illustrious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed One denoted by the syllable *ma*, whose nature is Śiva, Hanumān—*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, salutations again and again to him! || 3 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed the glorious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed Lord whose nature is the Bindu, the slayer of enemies (Śatrughna), the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svas—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 4 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed the illustrious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed Lord whose nature is sound, Bharata—the Earth, Atmosphere, and Heaven—to him indeed be salutation after salutation. || 5 ||
Oṃ! He who is indeed the glorious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, that Blessed One who is the very form of the Kalās, Lakṣmaṇa—homage again and again to him, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svas! || 6 ||

Oṃ! He who is indeed the glorious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa—the Blessed Lord—and the Blessed Goddess Sītā, who transcends the parts [of nature], whose nature is consciousness, [the source of] Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—to Him, indeed, be salutation after salutation. 7.
Just as it was stated regarding the first mantra, so it should be understood for all mantras:
the leader Hari, whose nature is Upendra, is denoted by the syllable *U*;
Hanumān, whose nature is Śiva, is denoted by the syllable *Ma*; Śatrughna, whose nature is the Bindu, is denoted by the [dot]; and [Lakṣmaṇa], whose nature is Nāda, is denoted by the [line].

Bharata is the embodiment of the arts (kalā), Lakṣmaṇa is beyond the arts (kalātīta), and the blessed Sītā is the embodiment of consciousness (cit). Oṃ! He who is indeed the glorious Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, he is the Blessed One, the Supreme, the Highest Person, the Ancient Supreme Puruṣa, eternally pure, awakened, liberated, and true.
I am Rāma, the Supreme Self, Brahman itself—supremely infinite, non-dual, and perfectly complete;
salutations again and again to Him who is Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ! || 8 ||

Whoever studies this eightfold mantra becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by the sun; he becomes purified by the sacrificial post (sthāṇu); he becomes known by all the gods. By him, the fruits of reciting one hundred thousand Rudra-hymns from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas have been attained.

By the recollection of the eight-syllabled mantra of the glorious Nārāyaṇa, one hundred thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī are accomplished; ten thousand recitations of the Praṇavas are accomplished. He purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants; he who knows this attains the state of Nārāyaṇa.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye fixed in the heavens.
The inspired poets, ever-vigilant and full of praise, kindle that supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
The third foot is the Sāmaveda. || 3 ||
Oṃ. That is fullness; this is fullness. From fullness, fullness arises. When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Tārasāropaniṣad.
